passage:
The bank branch opened at ten, and by 10:40 Neelam had already snapped at a customer about a form. The old man flinched. Her manager, Swati, called her into the small cabin.
'Third complaint this month, Neelam. And the team says you've been arguing about politics in the pantry. Loudly.'
Neelam wanted to defend herself. She was right, wasn't she? Everything she read at night said so. She'd been up till three again, reading, replying, raging. Her sister had stopped calling. Her best friend had muted her.
'This is a formal warning,' Swati said, not unkindly. 'You're good at this job. I don't want to lose you.'
Back at her counter, Neelam stared at the queue. She felt hollow. Not angry, for once. Just tired, down to her bones. She thought: when did I last feel anything but this?
It was a small, strange thought. She didn't push it away.

qa.q: What did Swati give Neelam?
qa.a: Swati gave her a formal warning.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling back at her counter?
qa.a: She felt hollow and deeply tired rather than angry, and began to wonder when she last felt anything else.

qa.q: What turning point might Neelam's tired, hollow moment open up?
qa.a: It could be the crack that lets doubt in; she could step back from the late-night reading, reconnect with her sister, and talk to a counsellor.

qa.q: How might the old customer have experienced Neelam's snapping?
qa.a: He probably felt startled and small, not knowing her anger had nothing to do with him.

grounding: It shows a young woman whose anger leaks into work, family and friendship, costing sleep and a warning, until exhaustion and emptiness let doubt in.

passage:
Dear Tanuja,
I got suspended today. Someone sent the office my posts. Two weeks without pay while they 'review'. I knew it was coming, honestly.
I'm writing because you're the only one who still replies. Ma won't talk politics with me any more; last Sunday I made her cry at lunch. Priyanka unfriended me. I'd called her 'part of the problem'.
I've been sleeping maybe four hours a night for months. I wake up already angry, before I've even looked at my phone.
And today, walking home, I felt this huge emptiness. Like I've been shouting for a year and there's nothing left. All that anger, and what has it changed? My life is smaller. My people are fewer.
I don't know what I believe right now. That scares me. But it's also the first time in a long time I've actually wanted to ask.
Can we meet this weekend?
Nikita

qa.q: How long is Nikita suspended without pay?
qa.a: Nikita is suspended for two weeks without pay.

qa.q: What does Nikita's line 'what has it changed?' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests exhaustion and emptiness after constant anger, and the first real doubt about the path Nikita has been on.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do at the weekend meeting to help?
qa.a: Tanuja could listen without saying 'I told you so', help Nikita think about sleep and stepping back from feeds, and suggest a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Ma feel if Nikita comes home and talks gently again?
qa.a: Ma may feel relief and hope, after being hurt at that Sunday lunch.

grounding: It shows a young person whose anger has cost a job, family peace, friendship and sleep, until exhaustion and emptiness open the first crack of doubt.

passage:
Chetan, you've been up again reading those threads; I can see it in your eyes. Let me tell you about Lalremsiami at twenty-five, in Aizawl, long before you knew me.
I was angry at one kind of person, and I spent every night online proving how bad they were. I stopped sleeping more than four hours. I snapped at my mother at dinner. I lost my closest friend, Mawii, because she questioned one post and I called her a coward in front of everyone.
Then my boss called me in. A client had seen my comments. They let me go that same week. I remember walking home in the rain, and the strange thing wasn't the anger. It was how empty I felt. So tired. As if the rage had eaten everything else.
That emptiness was the first crack. On that walk I finally asked myself what all of it had given me.
So now I'm asking you.

qa.q: How many hours was young Lalremsiami sleeping?
qa.a: Not more than four hours.

qa.q: What was young Lalremsiami feeling on the walk home in the rain?
qa.a: Young Lalremsiami felt empty and exhausted, as if the rage had eaten everything else.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let doubt in?
qa.a: The rainy walk home after losing the job, when exhaustion and emptiness led Lalremsiami to ask what the rage had given.

qa.q: How might Mawii have felt being called a coward?
qa.a: Mawii probably felt hurt and humiliated, pushed away by a close friend for asking one question.

grounding: An elder recalls how constant online rage cost sleep, a friendship and a job, and how the exhaustion finally let doubt in.

passage:
The HR email came at 6 p.m. on the eve of his sister's wedding: Jatin was suspended pending an inquiry into posts made from an account linked to his work profile. He read it in a corner of the decorated hall, fairy lights blinking above him.
For a year he had fought online every night, hundreds of comments about one group he blamed for everything. He hadn't slept properly in months.
Trisha found him there. "Your mother's looking for you. You haven't even greeted Chachi." Then she saw his face. "What happened?"
He showed her. She read it and said quietly, "I asked you to stop in March. You called me naive."
She went back inside to help with the garlands. Jatin sat alone, the music thumping through the wall. Under the anger he felt something he didn't recognise: plain exhaustion, and a small, cold question about what any of it had been for.

qa.q: When did the HR email come?
qa.a: At 6 p.m. on the eve of his sister's wedding.

qa.q: What did Jatin feel sitting alone as the music thumped?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and empty under the anger, with a small, cold doubt about what the rage had been for.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Jatin now?
qa.a: Letting the doubt in: apologising to Trisha, stepping away from the feeds, and getting help to understand how the anger took over.

qa.q: What is it like for Trisha at the wedding?
qa.a: Trisha feels hurt and weary, having warned him in March and been called naive, yet still helping the family.

grounding: On the eve of a family wedding a young man's online rage costs him his job and strains his relationship, and exhaustion opens a crack of doubt.

passage:
Rajni used to be the one who organised every family picnic. Now, in their Lucknow flat, her flatmate Zubin heard her typing at 3 a.m., jaw clenched, arguing with strangers about the people she was sure were ruining the country.
At dinner she corrected everyone and trusted no one. Her school friends' group chat had gone silent after she called them sheep. At the bank where she worked, her manager warned her twice about her phone at the counter. On Friday she was moved to the back office. "Temporary," they said.
On Saturday morning Zubin found her on the balcony, staring at nothing, still in yesterday's clothes.
"I'm so tired," she said. Not angry. Just tired. "I've been fighting for a year, and I don't even know what I've won."
Zubin sat down beside her with two cups of tea. He didn't say anything clever. He just stayed.

qa.q: Where was Rajni moved on Friday?
qa.a: To the back office.

qa.q: What does Rajni's 'I'm so tired' reveal?
qa.a: She feels exhausted and empty, the constant rage no longer giving her anything, which lets doubt in.

qa.q: What small steps could follow this moment on the balcony?
qa.a: Sleep, time away from the feeds, reconnecting with the school friends and perhaps talking to a counsellor about how the anger grew.

qa.q: What might Zubin feel sitting beside Rajni?
qa.a: Zubin probably feels worried but hopeful, sensing this tiredness might be the first opening.

grounding: A young woman's online anger costs her friendships, sleep and her job role, and her exhaustion becomes the crack that lets doubt in.

passage:
"You're shouting at the television again," Kunal said from the doorway.
"Because they're lying, Kunal! Look at this!" Ayesha held up her phone.
"It's two in the morning. You have the client call at nine."
"I'll manage."
"You said that last week. Then your manager emailed about the missed deadline."
"That's because I was up reading the truth, unlike you."
Kunal sat on the arm of the sofa. "Ammi called. She said you hung up on her on Sunday."
"She kept defending them."
"She asked about your cough, Ayesha."
Ayesha opened her mouth, then closed it. She looked at the screen, still scrolling by itself. "I'm so tired," she said quietly. "I'm angry all the time and I don't even feel better after."
"I know," Kunal said. "Come sleep. We can talk about it in the daylight."

qa.q: What time is it when Kunal comes to the doorway?
qa.a: It's two in the morning.

qa.q: What does Ayesha mean when she says she doesn't even feel better after being angry?
qa.a: She is exhausted and feels empty, and for the first time she is noticing that constant rage is costing her rather than helping.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Ayesha right now?
qa.a: She could go to sleep, then talk with Kunal in daylight about the costs to her work, health and family, and consider stepping back from the feeds or seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: How is Kunal affected by Ayesha's constant anger?
qa.a: Kunal is worried and tired too, watching her miss sleep, deadlines and calls with Ammi, but he stays patient so she can talk.

grounding: Shows anger leaking into family and work with lost sleep and job trouble, and the exhaustion of constant rage opening a crack for doubt.
